Description
The Coastal Conservation and Restoration Lab and the Coastal Water Health Lab at the Harte Research Institute for Gulf of Mexico Studies (HRI), Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi (TAMU-CC), are recruiting a Ph.D. student to investigate how changing freshwater inflows influence water quality and estuarine ecosystems along the Texas coast. The anticipated start date is Summer or Fall 2027.

The student will join a newly funded, multi-year project evaluating environmental flows across Texas. The project combines a statewide assessment of post-Senate Bill 3 environmental flows with intensive ecological and water-quality monitoring in the Nueces Estuary, providing opportunities to investigate questions spanning coast-wide patterns to local ecological responses.

The Ph.D. student will have substantial opportunities to develop and take ownership of dissertation questions within this broader framework. Potential research directions include coast-wide patterns in freshwater inflows and environmental-flow attainment; relationships among freshwater inflows, salinity, nutrients, primary productivity, water quality, and benthic communities; long-term ecological change; and development of biological indicators to support environmental-flow assessment and adaptive management.

Field research will include monthly water-quality sampling, quarterly benthic and sediment sampling, and targeted sampling following major freshwater inflow events or water-management changes. The student will also work with historical and contemporary environmental datasets to examine relationships among freshwater inflows, water quality, and ecological responses.

Qualifications: Applicants should have demonstrated research experience and a strong interest in estuarine or coastal science, including areas such as water quality, biogeochemistry, benthic ecology, or aquatic ecology. We are particularly interested in students who enjoy taking ownership of research questions, work well both independently and collaboratively, and approach research challenges with initiative, persistence, and creative problem-solving.

An M.S. degree in marine science, ecology, biology, environmental science, or a related field is preferred but not required for applicants with substantial equivalent research experience. Experience with field research, water-quality monitoring, benthic ecology, quantitative analysis/R, scientific writing, or environmental datasets is beneficial but not required.

The successful applicant will pursue a Ph.D. through the Coastal and Marine System Science (CMSS) or the Marine Biology (MARB) program at TAMU-CC and will be based at HRI in Corpus Christi, Texas.

The position includes a graduate research assistantship with a stipend of $2,000/month, increasing to $2,200/month upon advancement to candidacy, plus tuition, required fees, and health insurance.

To apply: Email Dr. Jennifer Beseres Pollack with (1) a CV, (2) unofficial transcripts, and (3) a brief email describing your research background and interests and why this opportunity interests you. Review of applications will begin immediately. For full consideration, materials should be received by December 15, 2026; the position will remain open until filled.
Contact
Jennifer Pollack
jennifer.pollack@tamucc.edu (preferred contact method)

M.S. Assistantship in Evaluating Professional Readiness in Wildlife, Fisheries, and Aquaculture 

We are seeking applicants for a funded Master’s assistantship to examine the professional readiness of wildlife, fisheries, and aquaculture graduates and the competency needs of employers across public, private, and non-profit natural resource sectors. The position is in the Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Aquaculture at Mississippi State University under the direction of Dr. Dan Pilgreen.

The successful applicant will contribute to all aspects of the research process, including survey development, data collection, stakeholder engagement, qualitative and quantitative data analysis, scientific writing, and dissemination of findings. Position Overview

The Department of Forestry and Environmental Resources at NC State University invites applications for a fully funded 4-year Graduate PhD Research Assistantship starting January 1, 2027. The student will lead interdisciplinary research evaluating how site-specific silvicultural interventions—specifically fertilization and understory vegetation control—influence loblolly pine (Pinus taeda L.) growth, landscape yield response, and economic returns under market and input cost uncertainty across the southeastern US.

The selected candidate will work at the intersection of quantitative forest ecology, remote sensing, and resource economics, collaborating closely with industry partners from the Forest Productivity Cooperative (FPC) and the Southern Forest Resource Assessment Consortium (SOFAC).

Key Responsibilities & Project Objectives
Growth Response Modeling (Objective 1): Quantify the magnitude, duration, and uncertainty of pine growth responses to fertilizer and herbicide treatments across 100+ empirical field trial sites, integrating soil, geology, climate, and competing vegetation drivers.
Remote Sensing & Spatial Scaling (Objective 2): Build reproducible workflows using open-source platforms to map growth responses and understory vegetation across 550 million acres, leveraging satellite imagery and LiDAR.
Economic Risk & Decision Modeling (Objective 3): Conduct spatially explicit financial assessments. Develop regime-switching stochastic dynamic models to evaluate optimal management choices amid volatile input costs, shifting stumpage prices, and local market shocks (e.g., mill closures).
Science Communication: Author peer-reviewed publications, present research at professional conferences, and engage with regional forestry stakeholders.

Technical Skills:
◦ Strong programming experience (e.g., R, Python) for geospatial processing and statistical modeling.
◦ Experience working with remote sensing datasets (LiDAR, satellite imagery, raster analytics).
◦ Knowledge of econometric analysis, Monte Carlo simulation, dynamic programming, or spatial growth-and-yield modeling is preferred.
Communication: Track record of scientific writing and clear communication with diverse academic and practitioner audiences.

The PATHWAYS Program (Partnerships Along the Headwaters of the Americas for Young Scientists) is a National Science Foundation International Research Experience for Students (IRES), run jointly by Washington State University and the University of New Mexico. It places U.S. graduate students in interdisciplinary research on water and social-ecological systems across Central and South America. Student research topics can include watersheds, the downstream water-use systems, or the societies embedded in them, including the adaptation challenges posed by changing hydro-climatic conditions. • Spring training (Jan–Apr): online coursework and cohort-building
• Summer school in Cuenca, Ecuador (May): a mandatory two-week, in-person session grounded in real-world water-governance challenges
• International research experience (typically Jun–Aug): fieldwork at the student's chosen host institution
• Fall synthesis (Sep–Dec): online meetings and cross-case comparison, culminating in a research presentation to the network

Funding covers travel to and from the summer school and the research site, a subsistence stipend of $1,500/month during the international research experience, and support for research expenses.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available with the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agriculture Research Service (ARS), located at Fort Collins, Colorado.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: During this appointment, you will have the opportunity to participate in projects focused on assessing the genetic diversity and how genetic diversity of pork quality changed from the 1990's to the present; determining the genetic uniqueness of chicken populations; and assessing genetic variability of cattle and swine semen samples placed under the stress of cryopreservation. 

Learning objectives: You will learn or enhance your current skillsets in the following:

Proficiency in genetic diversity analysis and trend evaluation
Expertise in assessing genetic uniqueness in livestock populations
Evaluation of genetic resilience under stress conditions, such as cryopreservation
Experience with advanced genetic assessment tools and methodologies using software programs such as ADMIXTURE, TreeMix, and GONe.

Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

The Department of Biology at William & Mary, a public university of the Commonwealth of Virginia, seeks applications for a tenure track position at the Assistant Professor level in Ecology. Appointment will begin August 10, 2027. We are interested in individuals with research and teaching expertise in ecology with a specialization in biostatistics and/or quantitative biology. Description
Ph.D. position in Aquatic Ecology – Ohio State University
 Hood Lab, Aquatic Ecology Laboratory, Department of Evolution, Ecology, and Organismal Biology, The Ohio State University
 The Hood Lab is recruiting a Ph.D. student to conduct research on a U.S. Department of Agriculture funded project that focuses on phosphorus cycling in ditches and streams in agriculture-dominated landscapes. The graduate student would join an interdisciplinary team focused on understanding how tile drainage impacts water, sediment, and nutrient dynamics. The student’s research would focus on determining how tile drains influence in-channel phosphorus storage and transformations. The project involves fieldwork in Ohio and Michigan as well as the use of sensors and game cameras to characterize dissolved oxygen, temperature, stream-channel form, and hydrologic characteristics. 
 The ideal candidate would have a Masters degree and be highly motivated and honest, with strong quantitative skills, an interest in applied aquatic ecology, and a background in ecology, biogeochemistry, soils, geomorphology, and/or hydrology. I seek to maintain a productive, diverse, and team-orientated lab group. 
 The student would be supported by teaching and research assistantships. In EEOB, graduate assistantship includes a stipend of at least $2,750 per month, health benefits, and a tuition/fee waiver.
 If interested, please email Jim Hood (hood.211@osu.edu) a single PDF containing (1) a statement of interest, (2) a CV, and (3) contact information for three references. I will begin reviewing candidate applications immediately and ultimately invite selected applicants to apply to the department. The department's application deadline is 15 Nov 2026.

Description
The Institute of Global Change Biology (IGCB) at the University of Michigan is seeking another round of exceptional applicants for the IGCB Michigan Postdoctoral Fellows Program. Successful applicants will have the opportunity and support to advance research in any aspect of global change biology.  They will also be able to participate in programs that include career mentoring, professional development, and academic networking opportunities. Applicants with interest across all areas of global change biology are invited to apply. For examples of previously funded projects, please see Research Fellows (past and present) on our website.

Faculty mentorship is a valued component of the IGCB Postdoctoral Fellows Program. The program requires regular collaboration and planning between Research Fellows and their mentors. We encourage applicants to contact at least two potential postdoc mentors at Michigan– we highly encourage co-mentoring. Preference will be given to applicants who bridge disciplines; co-mentoring across schools/departments is strongly encouraged. Co-funding of postdoc salaries (e.g. through grants to potential co-mentors or postdoc fellowships to candidates) is also encouraged but not expected. Potential mentors and their areas of interest are available on our website (see both the Steering Committee and Affiliated Faculty sections), although University of Michigan faculty mentors who are not yet affiliated with the IGCB will also be considered.

IGCB Michigan Postdoctoral Fellows are expected to be full participants in IGCB activities: including attending a weekly ‘Postdoc Plus’ group meeting and periodic IGCB seminars, workshops and training exercises; attending and/or presenting at annual IGCB Postdoc Plus, PhD student, and ‘all hands’ symposia; serving on the next IGCB Postdoc Fellows competition committee; providing timely updates for the IGCB website; and interacting in a variety of ways with other Fellows, and with IGCB Graduate Fellows  and Exchange Fellows.

The application deadline is September 30, 2026. Research in global change biology happens in many departments and units on campus, so Fellows could be jointly based in one of a number of departments and the IGCB. Successful applicants would be able to start their appointment as soon as feasible after a decision has been reached, but preferably not later than June 30, 2027 (although we can be flexible as needed). Most postdoc fellowships are expected to span two years; University protocols require a one-year initial appointment and subsequent evaluation. Postdocs of more than two years may be feasible when co-funding is available.

Applications must include: (1) A 1-page cover letter; (2) a CV; (3) names and contact information for three references; (4) a research statement. Research statements should include plans for proposed research and anticipated mentors at the University of Michigan (3 pages maximum, excluding references) and a short paragraph describing how the applicant’s research would fit in with and contribute to the IGCB Research Themes. Combine all parts of the application into a single PDF and upload the file in the application form here. Applicants should direct all three referees to upload their letters here.

Need additional information? See frequently asked questions and their responses here. Contact seas-igcb@umich.edu with any remaining inquiries.

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Great Lakes Coastal Environmental Science Laboratory, located in Duluth, Minnesota.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; national efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: The US EPA is mandated to address the endocrine disrupting potential of thousands of chemicals. For the majority of these chemicals there is a lack of information regarding whether they have the potential to cause adverse effects from impacts on thyroid hormone status. Understanding the important targets within the network of processes involved in maintaining normal functioning thyroid hormone levels, and what approaches to best assess activity at those targets are critical to developing a comprehensive approach to evaluating thyroid hormone disrupting potential of large numbers of chemicals.  

Recently, a number of thyroid-related in vitro high-throughput screening (HTS) assays have been developed to broaden assay coverage for molecular targets potentially leading to thyroid disruption and were implemented to screen US EPA’s ToxCast Phase 1, 2 and E1K chemical libraries. This battery of thyroid-related in vitro HTS assays can be employed to rapidly assess potential interference with these targets. However, this screening approach leaves uncertainties regarding the meaning of in vitro activity data as it relates to in vivo adverse outcomes. Part of this research effort aims to develop a translational process that integrates relevant information, models, and data streams to provide richer context to interpret in vitro results related to thyroid disruption. As part of the translational  process, this fellowship will focus on the development of a bio-assay to quantitative monitor thyroid hormone synthesis as a complimentary assay to existing in vitro thyroid-related assays. Assay development will be followed by the analysis of canonical and suspected thyroid disrupting chemicals to understand whether, or how, in vitro activity of chemicals translates to in vivo outcomes. Additionally, this research will employ existing computational tools such as the octanol-water partition coefficient (logKow) and quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSAR) models to provide deeper interpretation of in vitro data and further prioritize chemicals most likely to impact thyroid function in aquatic systems. The translational principles employed will have much broader applicability across ToxCast HTS assays and aquatic vertebrates. 

With guidance from the mentor, you may be involved in any or all of the following training activities:

Learn how innovative in vitro to in vivo extrapolation and reverse toxicokinetic approaches are used to translate effect concentrations measured in laboratory assays to equivalent blood, tissue, or environmental media concentrations.
Help with designing workflows and applying data analysis pipelines that support automated and standardized analysis of large scientific data sets.
Gain experience contributing to the development and implementation of data archiving and storage systems for research data management.
Learn how statistical and performance-based measures are applied to assess assay and data quality through quality assurance and quality control practices.
Process and analyze large, high-content data sets using established and emerging computational analysis pipelines under mentor guidance.
Compile and synthesize scientific information from peer-reviewed literature and online data sources to support interpretation of test results within the Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) framework.
Apply statistical analysis approaches such as hypothesis testing, regression methods, multivariate statistics, and concordance analyses to support research objectives.
Develop familiarity with computational and quantitative methods used in toxicology, exposure science, and data-intensive research environments.
Build scientific communication skills through preparation and presentation of research findings at regional, national, and international conferences or workshops.
Contribute to the preparation of peer-reviewed publications and dissemination materials for research partners, collaborators, and stakeholders.
Gain professional development experience in interdisciplinary research, data analysis, scientific collaboration, and communication of complex scientific findings to diverse audiences.
Learning Objectives: You will learn how to collaborate effectively within a transdisciplinary research team while gaining experience in project planning, scientific communication, research implementation, and data analysis activities. Through collaboration with researchers and staff, you will develop an understanding of how multidisciplinary scientific projects are designed, managed, and executed. You will also have opportunities to learn from and interact with internationally recognized scientific leaders within EPA and across external research organizations and institutions.

You will build knowledge of laboratory, analytical, and computational techniques that are broadly applicable across life sciences research fields. Through hands-on participation and mentorship, you will learn how to operate and use a variety of scientific instruments and equipment and gain familiarity with laboratory and research workflows. You will also learn approaches for evaluating data quality, troubleshooting research results, and applying statistical methods for scientific data analysis, interpretation, and communication. Opportunities may be available to contribute to original research efforts and support the development of scientific publications and related research products.

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Sigmund Degitz (degitz.sigmund@epa.gov). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor.

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: Fall 2026. All start dates are flexible and vary depending on numerous factors.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year and may be renewed three to four additional years upon EPA recommendation and subject to availability of funding.

Level of Participation: The appointment is full time.

Participant Stipend: The participant will receive a monthly stipend commensurate with educational level and experience. 

Citizenship Requirements: This opportunity is available to U.S. citizens and Lawful Permanent Residents (LPR) only.

EPA Security Clearance: Completion of a successful background investigation by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is required for an applicant to be on-boarded at EPA.

ORISE Information: This program, administered by ORAU through its contract with the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to manage the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education (ORISE), was established through an interagency agreement between DOE and EPA. Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5-year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility.

Questions: Please see the FAQ section of our website. If you have additional questions about the application process, please email ORISE.EPA.OCSPP@orau.org and include the reference code for this opportunity.

The qualified candidate should have received a master's or bachelor's degree in one of the relevant fields (Computational Biology, Computational Toxicology, Mathematics, Biostatistics, Computer Science). Degree must have been received within the past five years.

Candidates with a bachelors may be considered if they can demonstrate strong experience.

Experience designing workflows and applying data analysis pipelines for automated and standardized analysis of large data sets.
Experience developing and implementing a data archiving and storage system.
Experience identifying statistical and performance-based measures of assay and data quality and implementing quality assurance and quality control.
Experience processing and analyzing large, high content, data sets using both existing and novel computational pipelines.

Description
The Palmquist Lab at Marshall University is recruiting for a funded MS position at Marshall
University in vegetation dynamics and plant community change in coastal ecosystems. Our
research focuses on quantifying vegetation dynamics over space and time and identifying how
the relative importance of ecological processes structuring plant communities changes with
spatial and temporal scale. In addition, a key goal of our research is to understand how pattern
and process in plant communities will be altered in the face of global environmental change. An
important motivation for our work is to address ecological questions at large spatial scales to
inform landscape conservation. We collect field data, use existing large observational data sets,
and implement simulation modeling to address these goals in temperate shrublands, wetlands,
woodlands, and forests. Additional information about the lab can be found at
http://www.kylepalmquist.org/.

RESEARCH FOCUS: The successful candidate will explore plant community patterns and
short-term vegetation change and dynamics in coastal ecosystems on Marine Corps Recruit
Depot Parris Island (MCRDPI), a sea-island in South Carolina. Coastal vegetation provides
important ecosystem services, including storm protection, erosion control, and habitat for
wildlife. These complex, highly zoned plant communities are structured by multiple
environmental factors including salinity, elevation, soil texture, soil moisture, exposure, and light
availability. The project will leverage an existing network of 57 permanent vegetation plots
located throughout the island that were installed and sampled in 2022. The successful candidate
will re-sample these plots in summer 2027 to evaluate plant community change. In addition,
there is a rich plant community data set from 2022 that has yet to be fully explored. Finally, the
student will be able to leverage and potentially improve existing vegetation maps of the island
that were created from an integration of remotely sensed products and field validation points.

REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS: A background and relevant course work in plant ecology,
knowledge and experience with the vegetation of the southeastern US, strong communication
skills, and strong quantitative skills. Experience with plant community analysis and an interest in
questions that evaluate plant community patterns over space and time.

EXPECTATIONS: The successful candidate will be expected to conduct high-quality research,
serve as a teaching assistant within the Department of Biological Sciences, present their research
to the scientific community at regional and national meetings, and publish in peer-reviewed
scientific journals.

TIMELINE: The preferred start date is January 2027. The student must start no later than May
2027.

FUNDING: Funding will be provided by teaching assistantships for two years, along with
supplemental pay to conduct research during the academic year and summer. The 12-month pay
for this position is $24,000 and a full tuition waiver will be provided. The student is responsible
for covering University fees and health insurance.

HOW TO APPLY: Interested students should apply by submitting the following to Dr. Kyle
Palmquist (palmquist@marshall.edu): 1) short statement of research interests and career goals
(no longer than 1 page), 2) CV, 3) unofficial transcripts, and 4) contact information for threeprofessional references. Please include: “MS position – coastal vegetation” and your name in the email subject.

DEADLINE TO APPLY: No later than October 16, 2026.

Review of applications will begin immediately and continue until a candidate is selected. I will
contact you to discuss your research interests and goals for graduate school if I determine you
would be a good fit for the lab. If selected, a full application must be submitted to the
Department of Biological Sciences at Marshall University, Huntington, WV. Faculty in the
Department of Biological Sciences have expertise in a variety of biological fields, including but
not limited to ecology, evolution, herpetology, and physiology. More information about the
Department and its programs can be found here: https://www.marshall.edu/biology/. Application
requirements for admission to the DBS graduate program can be found here:
https://www.marshall.edu/biology/admission/.

Marshall University is located in Huntington, an affordable college town located on the Ohio
River in the beautiful state of West Virginia. The town is small enough to get around on foot and
bike, but large enough to support a variety of restaurants and other cultural activities. Huntington
and the surrounding area offer ample recreational opportunities (hiking, skiing, rafting), along
with proximity to larger cities, including Louisville, KY, Cincinnati, OH, and Columbus, OH. In
the Palmquist Lab, we highly value and encourage work-life balance.

I strongly encourage students from diverse backgrounds and experiences to apply. Feel free to
contact me with questions at any time.
Contact
Kyle Palmquist
palmquist@marshall.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
In the Department of Wildlife Sciences at the Faculty of Forestry Sciences and Forest Ecology, Georg-August-University Göttingen, the position of

Research Associate (f/m/d) 

is available as soon as possible within a third-party funded project focused on the further development of methods for genetic estimation of wildlife population sizes. The position is full-time (100% of regular weekly working hours, currently 39.8 hours per week). The position is initially limited until 30 June 2029, with the intention of extending it for a full three years. Remuneration is according to salary group 13 TV-L (this is the typical salary group for postdocs in Germany - it is enough money to live well). 
 

Position Description
In recent years, several methods for estimating wildlife population sizes based on the genetic identification of kinship relationships have been developed. These include, among others, Close-Kin Mark-Recapture (CKMR; see Sévêque et al. 2025, https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14490) and approaches involving the reconstruction of pedigrees (see Rosenblatt et al. 2023,  https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.10650). The successful candidate will further develop existing methods and adapt them for application to wild species commonly found in Germany that are subject to hunting. The initial focus will be on red deer (Cervus elaphus) and other ungulates, for which genetic samples can be collected via hunting. 

In addition to methodological development, you will use simulations to test the applicability of the method(s) under realistic conditions, and implemented the most promising approaches in R. 

There is also the opportunity to collaborate with researchers in the USA to test the methodology on a solitary carnivore species.

 Your Profile
We are seeking a highly motivated, productive, and independent individual with strong quantitative skills, particularly in statistical modeling. You possess…

-  a completed master's or diploma degree in a scientific field in Statistics, Modeling, Ecology, Genetics, Biology, or a closely related field  
- experience in statistical model development and coding  
- experience with simulation models  
- basic knowledge of population ecology  
- basic knowledge of population genetics  
- solid programming skills in R  
- excellent spoken and written English skills  
- experience in scientific writing, demonstrated by (co-)authorship of peer-reviewed articles in scientific journals  
- strong interest in wildlife ecology  

Advantageous are: a PhD in a relevant field, experience in statistical estimation of wildlife abundance—particularly using genetic methods—experience in determining kinship relationships using genetic markers, and knowledge of, or interest in, hunting-related topics.

Place of work is Göttingen. 

We offer flexible working conditions with significant potential for personal development.  

The University of Göttingen aims to increase the proportion of women in areas where they are underrepresented and therefore strongly encourages qualified women to apply. The university considers itself family-friendly and promotes the compatibility of academic work and family life. The university is particularly committed to the professional integration of disabled employees and welcomes applications from disabled persons. In cases of equal qualifications, applications from disabled persons will be given preference. Disability or equivalent status should be indicated in the application to safeguard your interests.


Please submit your clear, English-language application (including CV, cover letter, and copies of key certificates or employment references) as a single, continuous PDF document by 30.09.2026 to Agnieszka Melzer (wildlife@gwdg.de ). In your cover letter, please emphasize your relevant statistical expertise and, if applicable, your experience in abundance estimation.

For any questions about the position, please contact Niko Balkenhol (nbalken@gwdg.de).

Note:

By submitting your application, you consent to the processing of your personal data by us in accordance with data protection regulations. For more information on the legal basis and data usage, please see: [Information Sheet on the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)](https://uni-goettingen.de/DSGVO)

Contact
Niko Balkenhol
nbalken@gwdg.de (preferred contact method)
